analysis.one_liner: Creates a public Medicare-based health plan anyone can buy, and makes ACA premium subsidies permanent and richer.
analysis.headline: Introduced June 11, 2025 with 11 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill creates a new government-run health insurance plan, "Medicare Part E," that any U.S. resident can buy on the health exchanges, and that employers of any size can offer workers. It would pay doctors and hospitals at Medicare-negotiated rates, cover abortions even in states that ban them, ban balance billing by participating providers, and apply Medicare's prescription drug price negotiation to the plan. Alongside it, the bill makes Affordable Care Act premium subsidies permanent (removing the income cap that cuts families off), sweetens cost-sharing help for lower-income enrollees, caps traditional Medicare beneficiaries' out-of-pocket costs at $6,700 a year, puts $30 billion into a fund to lower premiums and out-of-pocket costs, and strengthens federal review of insurance rates.
analysis.who_benefits: People buying insurance on their own or through a small employer get a new, lower-priced government option paid at Medicare rates. Middle- and upper-middle-income families gain from permanent premium subsidies with no income cutoff. Lower-income marketplace enrollees get richer cost-sharing help. Traditional Medicare beneficiaries gain a $6,700 annual out-of-pocket cap, which Medicare currently lacks. Workers at employers with unaffordable health plans get a referral to enrollment help. Women in states with abortion restrictions get a plan that covers reproductive services regardless of state law.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Marketplace shoppers, Medicare beneficiaries, middle-income families

how_it_helps.text: Establishes Medicare Part E, a public health plan available in the individual, small group, and large group markets and sold on the federal and state exchanges [S2].

The plan is a gold-level qualified health plan covering all essential health benefits plus all Medicare-covered items and services, and it covers abortions and all other reproductive services even where state law would prohibit it [S2].

Providers are reimbursed at rates negotiated to be no lower, in aggregate, than Medicare rates and no higher than average exchange-plan rates, and all Medicare-participating providers are automatically in-network, with Medicare's balance-billing limits applied [S2].

Makes ACA premium tax credits permanent by removing the 400-percent-of-poverty income cap, and switches the subsidy benchmark from the second-lowest-cost silver plan to the second-lowest-cost gold plan, meaning richer subsidies [S2].
Expands cost-sharing reductions, raising insurers' share of allowed costs to as much as 94 percent for households near the poverty line and 80-90 percent for those up to 400 percent of poverty [S2].
Adds an annual out-of-pocket cap for traditional Medicare beneficiaries, $6,700 in 2027 and inflation-adjusted after that, beyond which Medicare pays the rest [S2].

Appropriates $30 billion for 2026-2028 for a state reinsurance and affordability fund to lower individual-market premiums and out-of-pocket costs, plus $2 billion in startup funding for the public plan [S2].
Requires employers whose coverage is unaffordable or lacks minimum value to refer full-time employees to exchange navigators, and funds expanded navigator capacity [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund the $2 billion startup appropriation, the $30 billion reinsurance and affordability fund, the permanent expansion of premium subsidies, and the new Medicare out-of-pocket cap. Hospitals, doctors, and other providers face Medicare-level payment rates for public-plan patients instead of higher commercial rates, with no balance billing allowed. Private insurers compete directly with a government plan priced at Medicare rates. Large employers face rating rules extended to the large group market and a new navigator-referral duty for plans deemed unaffordable.

drawbacks.text: The public plan is required to fully finance its own benefits and administrative costs through premiums, but startup funding ($2 billion) and initial claim reserves come from federal appropriations, and the subsidy enhancements and $30 billion reinsurance fund are direct federal spending [S2].

Hospitals and specialists who now receive commercial rates well above Medicare would be paid at Medicare-linked rates for public-plan patients, an honest supporter must acknowledge the reimbursement cut; the bill offsets this only by making all Medicare providers in-network to protect the plan's network breadth [S2].

A government plan priced below commercial insurers could draw healthier enrollees away from private plans, leaving private risk pools sicker and pricier; the bill's answer is the $30 billion reinsurance fund, which cushions private insurers with taxpayer money [S2].

Extending the small-group community-rating rules to the large group market removes employers' ability to vary premiums by health status in large plans, which supporters see as fairness and critics as a constraint on how employer plans are priced [S2].

The bill preempts state laws that prohibit coverage of abortions and other reproductive services, which is a substantial change in the balance between federal and state authority over insurance benefits [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the gains are large and concrete: a cheaper public option on every exchange, permanent subsidies without an income cliff, richer cost-sharing help, and the first-ever annual out-of-pocket cap in traditional Medicare. The main costs fall on hospitals and insurers (lower payment rates, real competition) and on taxpayers (roughly $32 billion in appropriations plus an unpriced permanent subsidy expansion). The design is more moderate than single-payer: it keeps private insurance intact and even pays insurers reinsurance subsidies, which is why critics from the left call it too timid and critics from the right call it a taxpayer-backed competitor to private business.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on June 11, 2025, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which has taken no further action on it; with Congress still in session, it is waiting with no hearing or vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Senator Merkley introduced S. 2032, the Choose Medicare Act, in the Senate on June 11, 2025 [S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance on the day it was introduced, the only action it has received [S4].
The bill has 11 cosponsors, all Democrats, including Senators Murphy, Baldwin, Blumenthal, Booker, Duckworth, Reed, Schatz, Gillibrand, and Smith [S3].
No Republicans have signed on, and the Senate Finance Committee has not scheduled a markup, so the bill has not moved toward a floor vote [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, private insurers, hospital systems, and drug makers are better off: the bill sits in committee, so no Medicare-priced public competitor, no Medicare out-of-pocket cap, and no permanent subsidy expansion exists, and the current insurance market structure continues unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers, hospitals, and drug makers

sides.party_line_note: All 12 named supporters, the sponsor and 11 cosponsors, are Democrats; no Republican has cosponsored, and with the bill stalled in committee there has been no recorded vote to show a broader split.

industries.note: A Medicare-priced public plan sold on the exchanges would compete directly with insurers' individual and group plans and could take customers from them. At the same time, the bill pays insurers $30 billion in reinsurance and affordability support and keeps subsidies flowing through private plans, so the industry's revenue is cushioned even as its market position is challenged.

Public-plan patients would be paid at Medicare-linked rates rather than higher commercial rates, and balance billing is barred, cutting provider revenue per patient. The offset is that every Medicare-participating provider is automatically in-network, guaranteeing volume and access for the new plan.

The bill applies Medicare's drug price negotiation provisions, including the excise tax for noncompliance, to drugs covered by the public plan, extending the negotiated prices the industry has fought to limit to Medicare's own program.

Employers of any size gain a new, potentially cheaper plan they can voluntarily offer workers, including having the government administer their group plan. In exchange, large-group plans come under small-group-style rating rules, and employers with unaffordable or bare-bones coverage must refer full-time workers to exchange enrollment help.

analysis.trajectory: A public-option bill sitting in the Senate Finance Committee with only Democratic support and no hearing or markup has almost never advanced to a floor vote in recent Congresses; unless the committee acts and 60 senators agree to take it up, this bill will likely die quietly at the end of the 119th Congress, though its subsidy-expansion and reinsurance ideas could be folded into larger health or tax legislation.
